question.knowledge_point: Finding the Points of Intersection of a Horizontal Line and a Tangent Curve
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14040762/assets/f00d8bd6cbd1f113df7f023e161e4d79e2f4a81157d1ac9a8ab65e70b4959221.png)

The graph above shows the curve $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ and the line $y=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.$  Find the $x$-coordinate of the point $B.$
question.worked_solution:
The $y$-values of both functions are the same at the intersection point. Equating the two equations gives: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}
$$

 Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})=-\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

This value lies inside $-\pi \le x<\pi $ hence, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}.$ This is the $x$ coordinate of $A.$

To get another solution, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Thus,

$$
{x}_{2}=\pi +x=\pi -\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{5\pi }{6}.
$$

So, the $x$-coordinate of $B$ is $\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

question.knowledge_point: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Tangent with Non-Special Angles
question.problem: Solve the equation $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=8$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ rounded to the nearest integer.
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(8)=82.874\,983{…}^{∘}≈{82.87}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${82.87}^{∘}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={82.87}^{∘}.$

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of ${180}^{∘}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}={180}^{∘}+{82.87}^{∘}={262.87}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are

$$
x={83}^{∘},{263}^{∘}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality Involving an Even Power Compared To a Negative Number
question.worked_solution:
Isolating the quadratic term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x+7)^{2}+4 & \le -6 \\ 2(x+7)^{2} & \le -10 \\ (x+7)^{2} & \le -5.\end{aligned}
$$

However, $(x+7)^{2}\ge 0$ for all values of $x$ because the power $(2)$ is even.

Therefore, there is no solution to the given inequality.

question.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{3}+7.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}+7}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}+7}}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{3}+7}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
question.worked_solution:
Let $u={x}^{3}-x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}-1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(3{x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}-1}{{x}^{3}-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}-x}\cdot (3{x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{3}-x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
question.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & =\frac{\sqrt{0+4}-2}{0}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\sqrt{x+4}-2)(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x+4-4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{0+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Acceleration Vector of a Particle Given Its Velocity Vector
question.problem:
The velocity vector $v=⟨u,v⟩$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
v=⟨5t-8,\,2{t}^{2}+4⟩.
$$

Calculate the acceleration vector $a.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t-8),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+4)⟩ \\  & =⟨5,\,4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Acceleration of a Particle at a Given Moment Given Its Velocity Vector
question.problem:
The velocity vector $v=⟨u,v⟩,$ measured in $\text{m}/\text{s},$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
v=⟨{2}^{t-1},\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}⟩.
$$

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=1.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t-1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1})⟩ \\  & =⟨{2}^{t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(1) & =⟨{2}^{1-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2(1)}{({1}^{2}+1)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨{2}^{0}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{2}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the magnitude of the acceleration, we compute $|a(1)|:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|a(1)| & =|⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-\frac{1}{2}⟩| \\  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{ln}^{2}⁡2+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4{ln}^{2}⁡2+1}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4{ln}^{2}⁡2+1}}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Acceleration of a Particle at a Given Moment Given Its Velocity Vector
question.problem:
The velocity vector $v=⟨u,v⟩,$ measured in $\text{m}/\text{s},$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
v=⟨-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{8}.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration at time $t=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we substitute $t=\frac{\pi }{8}$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}),2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})⟩ \\  & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨4\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},2\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨4,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the magnitude of the acceleration, we compute $|a(\frac{\pi }{8})|:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|a(\frac{\pi }{8})| & =|⟨4,2⟩| \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+4} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Acceleration Vector of a Particle Given Its Position Vector
question.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\frac{{t}^{5}}{5},\,3{t}^{2}-1⟩.
$$

Calculate the acceleration vector $a.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4},\,6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Acceleration Vector of a Particle Given Its Position Vector
question.problem:
The position vector $r(t)$ of a particle $P$ relative to a fixed origin $O$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1,{e}^{2t+5}⟩.
$$

Calculate the acceleration vector $a.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t+5})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,2{e}^{2t+5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{2t+5})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,4{e}^{2t+5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Acceleration of a Particle at a Given Moment Given Its Position Vector
question.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨4-2{t}^{2},1-3{t}^{3}⟩.
$$

Calculate the acceleration vector $a$ at time $t=1.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-2{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-3{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t,-9{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-4t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-9{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,-18t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the acceleration at time $t=1,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(1) & =⟨-4,-18(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,-18⟩\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
question.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3{cos}^{2}⁡x+1-3{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int [3({cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)+1]\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =3(\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+x+C \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining the Equation of a Tall Ellipse
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14041013/assets/be8468d84e3820bd1e9181d31aa3a1b7d1a85c743020a69cb67fc3f601a88363.png)

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?
question.worked_solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=2$ and the vertical radius has length $b=5.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
